items.title: 67260_Freddie Moore oral history interview
items.q: I know about him! In that style.

ctx.x: the drummers were doing or what they were not doing? Say, Dizzy Come... You were playing music before Dizzy was born or before Charlie Parker was born. So they were coming in, it seemed, with a new sound. Did much of that impress you in any way, or was it something that didn't really...it wasn't very important to you?
One of the main drummers who used to play with Dizzy, that drummer I just mentioned a while ago...

items.title: 67260_Freddie Moore oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee mentions 'One of the main drummers who used to play with Dizzy' but does not state he played with or met Dizzy himself; the interviewer notes the interviewee was playing before Dizzy was born.

ctx.x: Well, I didn't get the opportunity to meet too many of the younger drummers. Like Kenny Clarke, he was a very good drummer. And there was a drummer who was living over... I think he passed away. He was in Paris there for a while. But he wasn't necessarily a younger drummer; but he had a lot of experience. It will come to me after a while, what that boy's name is over in Paris, France. He had just come out of the Army.

Well, a lot of the... Max Roach and Kenny Clarke are two of the drummers who, being involved with the music of, say, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Come, also paid a great deal of respect to Big Sid Catlett. Had you heard about this new musical style from the musicians who might get together and just have your (?) sessions, or you'd be talking about music and musicians? Did you talk about what
